claim: Rapid, moment to moment, fluctuations in arousal state occur across species, from mice to humans.
source: Rapid, moment to moment, fluctuations in arousal state occur across species, from mice to humans, and have a significant impact on both cortical/subcortical activity and the ability to perform behavioral tasks (reviewed in Flavell et al., 2022; Lee and Dan, 2012; McCormick et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Rapid, moment to moment, fluctuations in arousal state have a significant impact on both cortical/subcortical activity and the ability to perform behavioral tasks.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: In mice, rapid behavioral state fluctuations are coupled with broad changes in cortical excitation.

evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

source: The basal forebrain-derived cholinergic (BF-ACh) system is topographically organized such that subregions within the BF preferentially project to different cortical and subcortical targets (Gielow and Zaborszky, 2017; Huppé-Gourgues et al., 2018; Zaborszky et al., 2015), and activation of distinct regions of the BF results in desynchronization of restricted cortical regions (Kim et al., 2016).

source: The basal forebrain-derived cholinergic (BF-ACh) system is topographically organized such that subregions within the BF preferentially project to different cortical and subcortical targets (Gielow and Zaborszky, 2017; Huppé-Gourgues et al., 2018; Zaborszky et al., 2015), and activation of distinct regions of the BF results in desynchronization of restricted cortical regions (Kim et al., 2016).

claim: Many superficial layer VIP interneurons exhibit activity related to arousal/movement.
source: While many superficial layer VIP interneurons exhibit activity related to arousal/movement (Dipoppa et al., 2018; Fu et al., 2014; Munoz et al., 2017; Petersen, 2019; Poulet and Crochet, 2018; Reimer et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2019), it is unclear how homogeneous or heterogeneous the activity of cholinergic VCINs is in association with arousal or behavioral (e.g. movement) state.

source: While many superficial layer VIP interneurons exhibit activity related to arousal/movement (Dipoppa et al., 2018; Fu et al., 2014; Munoz et al., 2017; Petersen, 2019; Poulet and Crochet, 2018; Reimer et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2019), it is unclear how homogeneous or heterogeneous the activity of cholinergic VCINs is in association with arousal or behavioral (e.g. movement) state.

claim: Within the locus coeruleus-derived noradrenergic (LC-NA) system, synchronized activity between LC neurons is often observed in relation to increases in behavioral engagement/vigilance to external events or stimuli.
source: Within the locus coeruleus-derived noradrenergic (LC-NA) system, synchronized activity between LC neurons is often observed in relation to increases in behavioral engagement/vigilance to external events or stimuli (reviewed in Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Poe et al., 2020; Sara, 2009), while modularity is strongly suggested by evidence of topographically distinct projection patterns (Chandler et al., 2014; Kebschull et al., 2016; Loughlin et al., 1986; Loughlin et al., 1982; Waterhouse et al., 1983) and paired recordings in the rat LC which can show little synchrony in spontaneous or evoked activity, at least under conditions of anesthesia (Noei et al., 2022; Totah et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Modularity in the LC-NA system is strongly suggested by evidence of topographically distinct projection patterns.
source: Within the locus coeruleus-derived noradrenergic (LC-NA) system, synchronized activity between LC neurons is often observed in relation to increases in behavioral engagement/vigilance to external events or stimuli (reviewed in Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Poe et al., 2020; Sara, 2009), while modularity is strongly suggested by evidence of topographically distinct projection patterns (Chandler et al., 2014; Kebschull et al., 2016; Loughlin et al., 1986; Loughlin et al., 1982; Waterhouse et al., 1983) and paired recordings in the rat LC which can show little synchrony in spontaneous or evoked activity, at least under conditions of anesthesia (Noei et al., 2022; Totah et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Paired recordings in the rat LC can show little synchrony in spontaneous or evoked activity, at least under conditions of anesthesia.
source: Within the locus coeruleus-derived noradrenergic (LC-NA) system, synchronized activity between LC neurons is often observed in relation to increases in behavioral engagement/vigilance to external events or stimuli (reviewed in Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Poe et al., 2020; Sara, 2009), while modularity is strongly suggested by evidence of topographically distinct projection patterns (Chandler et al., 2014; Kebschull et al., 2016; Loughlin et al., 1986; Loughlin et al., 1982; Waterhouse et al., 1983) and paired recordings in the rat LC which can show little synchrony in spontaneous or evoked activity, at least under conditions of anesthesia (Noei et al., 2022; Totah et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Recent investigations in awake, behaving mice reveal some level of heterogeneity in neuronal activity between different LC neurons in relation to behaviorally relevant components on learned and rewarded tasks.
source: Recent investigations in awake, behaving mice reveal some level of heterogeneity in neuronal activity between different LC neurons in relation to behaviorally relevant components on learned and rewarded tasks (Breton-Provencher et al., 2022; Uematsu et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A broadly synchronized, arousal and/or behavioral state-dependent component of cholinergic and noradrenergic activity may operate alongside a more local, task-specific component.
source: Together, evidence suggests that a broadly synchronized, arousal and/or behavioral state-dependent component of cholinergic and noradrenergic activity may operate alongside a more local, task-specific component.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the evidence presented in the preceding paragraphs.

claim: During spontaneous behavior, cholinergic and noradrenergic signaling is dominated by a global (cortex-wide) component that is strongly predicted by arousal-related behavior.
source: Here, through simultaneous imaging of GCaMP6s expressed in multiple ACh or NA axons (and local cholinergic interneurons) across the dorsal cortex, we find that, during spontaneous behavior, cholinergic and noradrenergic signaling is dominated by a global (cortex-wide) component that is strongly predicted by arousal-related behavior.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study as stated in the introduction.

claim: Injections of an axon-targeted GCaMP6s calcium sensor were made into the BF to image BF-ACh axons.
source: To image BF-ACh axons, injections of an axon-targeted GCaMP6s calcium sensor were made into the BF (N = 5 mice, n = 397 axon segments; see 'Materials and methods'; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: To image NA axons originating from the LC, a cre-dependent, transgenically encoded GCaMP6s calcium reporter line was crossed with a DBH-cre line.
source: To image NA axons originating from the LC (Giustino and Maren, 2018), a cre-dependent, transgenically encoded GCaMP6s calcium reporter line was crossed with a DBH-cre line (N = 6 mice, n = 283 axon segments; see 'Materials and methods'; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: Both cholinergic and noradrenergic axon GCaMP6s activity increased markedly in relation to whisker pad movement (twitching or whisking) and walking.
source: Both cholinergic and noradrenergic axon GCaMP6s activity increased markedly in relation to whisker pad movement (twitching or whisking) and walking (Figure 1D–G; Video 1).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figures and video.

claim: A striking similarity was apparent between the patterns of activity in different axons, even if these axon segments were from distant recording locations.
source: A striking similarity was apparent between the patterns of activity in different axons, even if these axon segments were from distant recording locations.
evidence: This is an observation from the data presented in the figures.

claim: GCaMP6s activity in the noradrenergic axon segments was more transient than in cholinergic axon segments during a prolonged walking bout.
source: While both cholinergic and noradrenergic axons exhibited activity that was clearly related to behavioral state (as measured by whisker movements and walking), there was also an apparent difference between these two systems. GCaMP6s activity in the noradrenergic axon segments was more transient than in cholinergic axon segments during a prolonged walking bout (Figure 1E and G; see also Figure 2D and E), consistent with previous reports (see also below; Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figures and is consistent with previous reports.

claim: At the onset of both facial movements/twitches, as well as whisking bouts, both BF-ACh and LC-NA axonal activity sharply increased.
source: At the onset of both facial movements/twitches, as well as whisking bouts (which involve both larger and more prolonged movements of the whiskers than whisker twitches), both BF-ACh and LC-NA axonal activity sharply increased (Figure 2A and B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: No change in fluorescence was observed at the onset of whisking in either autofluorescent blebs or non-activity-dependent mCherry axon fluorescence.
source: Importantly, no change in fluorescence was observed at the onset of whisking in either autofluorescent blebs (Figure 2A and B) or non-activity-dependent mCherry axon fluorescence (Figure 2F, Video 2).
evidence: This control experiment confirms that the observed changes are not due to motion artifacts.

claim: The onset of the increases in average BF-ACh and LC-NA axonal activity occurred, on average, nearly simultaneously with the onset of whisking.
source: Expanding the time base revealed that the onset of the increases in average BF-ACh and LC-NA axonal activity occurred, on average, nearly simultaneously with the onset of whisking (Figure 2B, insets).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Both cholinergic and noradrenergic axon activity decreased along with whisker movement just prior to onset of whisker twitches or a bout of whisking.
source: Both cholinergic and noradrenergic axon activity decreased along with whisker movement just prior to onset of whisker twitches or a bout of whisking (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: At the cessation of facial movement, BF-ACh and LC-NA axon activity decreased slowly (over 1–2 s), in comparison to the rapid rise at movement onset.
source: At the cessation of facial movement, BF-ACh and LC-NA axon activity decreased slowly (over 1–2 s; Figure 2B, offset), in comparison to the rapid rise at movement onset (Figure 2B, onset).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Cholinergic fibers exhibit more sustained responses than noradrenergic axons during a bout of walking.
source: Previous studies of cholinergic and noradrenergic axonal GCaMP activity revealed that cholinergic fibers exhibit more sustained responses than noradrenergic axons during a bout of walking (Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Cholinergic axonal GCaMP6s responses are significantly more sustained than the noradrenergic axonal responses during whisking bouts of different durations.
source: By examining whisking bouts of different durations, from 1 s to >5 s, we also observed that cholinergic axonal GCaMP6s responses are significantly more sustained than the noradrenergic axonal responses (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: During prolonged (>5 s) bouts of whisking, the NA axonal response typically exhibited a strong increase in GCaMP6s fluorescence at the beginning of the whisking bout, which decreased over the next 0.5–1.5 s to a steady value that was on average 11% of the peak value.
source: For example, during prolonged (>5 s) bouts of whisking, the NA axonal response typically exhibited a strong increase in GCaMP6s fluorescence at the beginning of the whisking bout, which decreased over the next 0.5–1.5 s to a steady value that was on average 11% of the peak value (activity at 2–3 s compared to peak, t = –15.14, p<0.0001; Figure 2E).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figure and statistical analysis.

claim: Cholinergic fibers exhibited a more sustained response during prolonged whisking bouts, such that the activity 2–3 s into the prolonged whisking bout was 93% of the peak.
source: In contrast, cholinergic fibers exhibited a more sustained response, such that the activity 2–3 s into the prolonged whisking bout was 93% of the peak (activity at 2–3 s compared to peak, t = 0.91, p=0.36; Figure 2D).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figure and statistical analysis.

claim: The GCaMP6s activity of both BF-ACh and LC-NA axons increased prior to the onset and slowly decreased at the offset, of a walking bout.
source: The GCaMP6s activity of both BF-ACh and LC-NA axons increased prior to the onset and slowly decreased at the offset, of a walking bout (Figure 2C).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: A large number of BF-ACh and LC-NA axons increased activity at the onset of twitching (BF-ACh: 44.2 ± 30.9%; LC-NA: 47.3 ± 28.4%) and whisking (BF-ACh: 78.8 ± 23.5%; LC-NA: 67.3 ± 30.9%) bouts.
source: We found that a large number of BF-ACh and LC-NA axons increased activity at the onset of twitching (BF-ACh: 44.2 ± 30.9%; LC-NA: 47.3 ± 28.4%) and whisking (BF-ACh: 78.8 ± 23.5%; LC-NA: 67.3 ± 30.9%) bouts.
evidence: This finding is based on analysis of the probability of axonal responses to behavioral events.

claim: On average, each BF-ACh axon significantly increased activity on 43.5 ± 15.7% of twitching and 75.8 ± 25.0% of whisking bouts.
source: On average, each BF-ACh axon significantly increased activity on 43.5 ± 15.7% of twitching and 75.8 ± 25.0% of whisking bouts.
evidence: This finding is based on analysis of the probability of axonal responses to behavioral events.

claim: On average, each LC-NA axon segment significantly increased activity on 46.7 ± 13.7% of twitching and 74.4 ± 24.4% of whisking bouts.
source: Similarly, on average, each LC-NA axon segment significantly increased activity on 46.7 ± 13.7% of twitching and 74.4 ± 24.4% of whisking bouts.
evidence: This finding is based on analysis of the probability of axonal responses to behavioral events.

claim: With each whisker twitch, approximately half of NA and ACh axons will show increased activity responses, while with the transition to full whisking ~75% of NA and ACh axons are activated.
source: These results indicate that, on average, with each whisker twitch, approximately half of NA and ACh axons will show increased activity responses, while with the transition to full whisking ~75% of NA and ACh axons are activated.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings on axonal response probabilities.

claim: Whisker pad movement is consistently initiated, with a variable onset, 0.5–5 s prior to walking initiation and typically persists for approximately 1–3 s, with a variable offset, after the cessation of walking.
source: We observed that whisker pad movement is consistently initiated, with a variable onset, 0.5–5 s prior to walking initiation and typically persists for approximately 1–3 s, with a variable offset, after the cessation of walking (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figure supplement.

claim: The lack of tight temporal correlation between onset/offset of walking with cholinergic and noradrenergic activity is likely the result of a variable timing of onset/offset of whisking/arousal in relationship to walking bouts, and the strong association between ACh and NA axonal activity and behavioral state.
source: Thus, the lack of tight temporal correlation between onset/offset of walking with cholinergic and noradrenergic activity is likely the result of a variable timing of onset/offset of whisking/arousal in relationship to walking bouts, and the strong association between ACh and NA axonal activity and behavioral state (which is tightly linked to whisker movements; Figure 1E and G).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on the observed temporal relationships.

claim: Coherence between both BF-ACh and LC-NA axon activity and facial movement and pupil diameter was highest at low frequencies (<1 Hz).
source: In similarity to these studies, we found that coherence between both BF-ACh and LC-NA axon activity and facial movement and pupil diameter was highest at low frequencies (<1 Hz; Figure 3C).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: In comparison to walking speed and pupil dilation, a stronger coherence was observed between both BF-ACh and LC-NA axon activity and facial movements (including snout, jaw, whisker pad, and full face motion energy).
source: However, in comparison to walking speed and pupil dilation, we observed a stronger coherence between both BF-ACh and LC-NA axon activity and facial movements (including snout, jaw, whisker pad, and full face motion energy; Figure 3C and D), suggesting that facial movement is tightly coupled to changes in cholinergic and noradrenergic signaling in the cortex.
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Facial movement is tightly coupled to changes in cholinergic and noradrenergic signaling in the cortex.
source: However, in comparison to walking speed and pupil dilation, we observed a stronger coherence between both BF-ACh and LC-NA axon activity and facial movements (including snout, jaw, whisker pad, and full face motion energy; Figure 3C and D), suggesting that facial movement is tightly coupled to changes in cholinergic and noradrenergic signaling in the cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the coherence analysis.

claim: The large drop in coherence between axonal activity and measures of behavioral state at frequencies above approximately 1 Hz likely represents more of a limitation of the imaging method to detect axonal activity at frequencies above 1–2 Hz, than a true lack of coherence.
source: The large drop in coherence between axonal activity and measures of behavioral state at frequencies above approximately 1 Hz likely represents more of a limitation of our imaging method to detect axonal activity at frequencies above 1–2 Hz, than a true lack of coherence (see Figure 4A–E and 'Materials and methods'; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the coherence data based on the limitations of the imaging method.

claim: The temporal relationship between BF-ACh activity and facial movement was closely time-locked such that axonal activity was observed very shortly (within 100–200 ms) following the onset of facial movements.
source: The temporal relationship between BF-ACh activity and facial movement, as measured by cross-correlation, was closely time-locked such that axonal activity was observed very shortly (within 100–200 ms) following the onset of facial movements (Figure 3E).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The delay between facial movement onset and BF-ACh activity is approximately the same as the rise-time required for GCaMP6s to bind Ca2+ and fluoresce in response to the initiation of action potentials (100–150 ms).
source: This delay is approximately the same as the rise-time required for GCaMP6s to bind Ca2+ and fluoresce in response to the initiation of action potentials (100–150 ms; Chen et al., 2013), indicating that the behavioral state-dependent onset of facial movements and increased activity in the BF-ACh system occurred within a relatively short time period, beyond our ability to resolve (see also Figure 2B insets).
evidence: This comparison is based on known GCaMP6s kinetics from a cited study.

claim: The full model accounted for 33.3 ± 2.9% of variance in BF-ACh axonal activity.
source: The full model accounted for 33.3 ± 2.9% of variance in BF-ACh axonal activity (Figure 3F).
evidence: This finding is based on ridge regression analysis.

claim: Movement of the whisker pad area explained more of the variance in BF-ACh axonal activity than any other variable (whisker pad movement explained variance = 24.1 ± 2.8%; F = 89.2, p<0.0001).
source: Movement of the whisker pad area explained more of the variance in BF-ACh axonal activity than any other variable (whisker pad movement explained variance = 24.1 ± 2.8%; F = 89.2, p<0.0001; one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This finding is based on ridge regression analysis and statistical testing.

claim: Walking speed explained less variance in BF-ACh axon activity than any other behavioral measure (R2 = –0.05 ± 0.02).
source: Walking speed explained less variance in axon activity than any other behavioral measure (R2 = –0.05 ± 0.02).
evidence: This finding is based on ridge regression analysis.

claim: Activity of LC-NA axons lagged facial movements by 100–200 ms.
source: Similar to BF-ACh, activity of LC-NA axons lagged facial movements by 100–200 ms and facial (whisker, snout, full face) movements explained more variance in the noradrenergic axonal signal than walking speed or pupil diameter (Figure 3G and H; F = 17.16, p<0.0001).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figures and statistical analysis.

claim: Facial (whisker, snout, full face) movements explained more variance in the noradrenergic axonal signal than walking speed or pupil diameter (F = 17.16, p<0.0001).
source: Similar to BF-ACh, activity of LC-NA axons lagged facial movements by 100–200 ms and facial (whisker, snout, full face) movements explained more variance in the noradrenergic axonal signal than walking speed or pupil diameter (Figure 3G and H; F = 17.16, p<0.0001).
evidence: This finding is based on ridge regression analysis and statistical testing.

claim: For both BF-ACh and LC-NA data sets, prediction error for matched whisking and walking data sets was low in comparison to the distribution of unmatched sessions.
source: For both BF-ACh and LC-NA data sets, prediction error for matched whisking and walking data sets was low in comparison to the distribution of unmatched sessions; therefore, we conclude that the relationships determined by linear regressions are valid (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is based on the session permutation method to validate the regression results.

claim: A high average correlation was found between GCaMP6s activity in both cholinergic and noradrenergic axon segments (ACh: 0.54 ± 0.19; NA: 0.44 ± 0.15).
source: Overall, we found a high average correlation between GCaMP6s activity in both cholinergic and noradrenergic axon segments (ACh: 0.54 ± 0.19; NA: 0.44 ± 0.15).
evidence: This finding is based on correlation analysis of axonal activity.

claim: A broad distribution of correlations was observed that slightly decreased (for ACh axon segments) with distance, suggesting that heterogeneous signals may also be present.
source: However, we also observed a broad distribution of correlations that slightly decreased (for ACh axon segments), with distance, suggesting that heterogeneous signals may also be present (described below).
evidence: This is an observation from the correlation analysis.

claim: Comparing the average coherence between all cholinergic/noradrenergic axon segments revealed a high coherence at frequencies less than approximately 1 Hz, and this group average coherence decreased markedly at frequencies above approximately 1 Hz.
source: Comparing the average coherence between all cholinergic/noradrenergic axon segments revealed a high coherence at frequencies less than approximately 1 Hz, and this group average coherence decreased markedly at frequencies above approximately 1 Hz (Figure 4D and E, Exp. data).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The high level of average coherence between simultaneously imaged cholinergic/noradrenergic axon segments at frequencies <1 Hz suggests the presence of a strong common signal that is broadly expressed across these segments.
source: This high level of average coherence between simultaneously imaged cholinergic/noradrenergic axon segments at frequencies <1 Hz suggests the presence of a strong common signal that is broadly expressed across these segments (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the coherence data.

claim: The drop off in coherence at frequencies >1 Hz is most likely a consequence of the frequency limitations of the data collection technique.
source: The drop off in coherence at frequencies >1 Hz is most likely a consequence of the frequency limitations of our data collection technique (see below and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the limitations of the imaging method.

claim: Plotting the residual partial correlation versus the ordinary (full) correlation revealed a large decrease in correlation for the vast majority of axon segments when the common signal is taken into account, such that the partial correlation centered around approximately 0 (ACh: mean = 0.03 ± 0.14 [SD]; NA: 0.07 ± 0.11).
source: Plotting the residual partial correlation versus the ordinary (full) correlation revealed a large decrease in correlation for the vast majority of axon segments when this common signal is taken into account, such that the partial correlation centered around approximately 0 (ACh: mean = 0.03 ± 0.14 [SD]; NA: 0.07 ± 0.11; Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This finding is based on partial correlation analysis.

claim: Much of the ordinary correlation between axon segments, particularly at values below approximately 0.5–0.6, may have resulted from the correlation of the two axon segments to a common signal related to behavioral state.
source: This result indicates that much of the ordinary correlation between axon segments, particularly at values below approximately 0.5–0.6, may have resulted from the correlation of the two axon segments to a common signal related to behavioral state.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the partial correlation analysis results.

claim: Examining the fluorescence of non-activity-dependent mCherry-labeled axons did not reveal a significant decrease with partial (vs. ordinary) correlation, indicating that the effect observed in cholinergic and noradrenergic axons with this comparison is not due to movement-artifacts.
source: Examining the fluorescence of non-activity-dependent mCherry-labeled axons did not reveal a significant decrease with partial (vs. ordinary) correlation, indicating that the effect observed in cholinergic and noradrenergic axons with this comparison is not due to movement-artifacts (Figure 4H).
evidence: This control experiment confirms that the observed effects are not due to motion artifacts.

claim: Removing periods of both walking and whisking significantly (p<0.01) lessened the difference between the partial and ordinary correlations, while removing periods of walking did not have a significant effect.
source: We found that removing periods of both walking and whisking significantly (p<0.01) lessened the difference between the partial and ordinary correlations, while removing periods of walking did not have a significant effect (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This finding is based on analysis of correlations during different behavioral states and statistical testing.

claim: A significant portion of the common signal in ACh and NA axon activity results from behavioral state variations associated with movements.
source: This result confirms that a significant portion of the common signal in ACh and NA axon activity results from behavioral state variations associated with movements.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of correlations during different behavioral states.

claim: The distribution of coherence values between simultaneously monitored axon segments was substantially broader than that observed in pairs of segments from the same axon.
source: The distribution of coherence values was substantially broader than that observed in pairs of segments from the same axon (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The average correlations between ACh axon segments decreased weakly with increased distance between segments.
source: The average correlations between ACh axon segments decreased weakly with increased distance between segments (Figure 4J), with the correlation between inter-axonal segment activity correlation and distance between segments being –0.12 (p<0.001).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figure and statistical analysis.

claim: There was no significant relationship between distance and correlation between NA axon segments (r = 0.02; p=0.46).
source: In contrast, there was no significant relationship between distance and correlation between NA axon segments (r = 0.02; p=0.46; Figure 4K).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figure and statistical analysis.

claim: The distributions of residual correlations between heterogeneous cholinergic, noradrenergic, or non-activity-dependent mCherry axons were nearly identical.
source: Interestingly, the distributions of residual correlations between heterogeneous cholinergic, noradrenergic, or non-activity-dependent mCherry axons were nearly identical (Figure 4Q).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: No statistical differences were found between the distributions of residual correlations for cholinergic, noradrenergic, and mCherry axons (p>0.001; F = 76.98; one-way ANOVA).
source: We found no statistical differences between these distributions (p>0.001; F = 76.98; one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This finding is based on statistical testing of the distributions.

claim: Comparing the distribution of partial (residual) correlations between cholinergic axons revealed a significant distance dependence (r = −0.4; p<0.01), such that axon segments within the same ROI exhibited a higher correlation than axon segments that were more distant.
source: However, comparing the distribution of partial (residual) correlations between cholinergic axons revealed a significant distance dependence (r = −0.4; p<0.01), such that axon segments within the same ROI exhibited a higher correlation than axon segments that were more distant (Figure 4N).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figure and statistical analysis.

claim: In noradrenergic axon segments, the partial (residual) correlation decreased slightly with distance, dropping from 0.09 ± 0.12 within the same ROI, to 0.06 ± 0.10 between all other axon segment pairs.
source: In noradrenergic axon segments, the partial (residual) correlation decreased slightly with distance, dropping from 0.09 ± 0.12 within the same ROI, to 0.06 ± 0.10 between all other axon segment pairs (Figure 4O).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The overall correlation between distance and residual partial correlation for NA axon segments was very low, but statistically significant (r = –0.10; p<0.001).
source: The overall correlation between distance and residual partial correlation for NA axon segments was very low, but statistically significant (r = –0.10; p<0.001).
evidence: This finding is based on statistical analysis of the relationship between distance and partial correlation.

claim: No change in partial correlation was observed with increasing distance for non-activity-dependent mCherry axons (r = –0.03; p=0.35).
source: We confirmed that artifactual movement within the imaging field was not driving distance-dependent changes in partial correlations by comparing partial correlations between non-activity-dependent mCherry axons across distance. No change in partial correlation was observed with increasing distance (Figure 4P; r = –0.03; p=0.35).
evidence: This control experiment confirms that the observed effects are not due to motion artifacts.

claim: There is a strong correlation and coherence between axon segments of cholinergic and noradrenergic axons within the cerebral cortex, that these correlations extend for long distances (at least 3.5–4 millimeters), and that the major contributor to these correlations is a common signal related to behavioral state.
source: Our results indicate that there is a strong correlation and coherence between axon segments of cholinergic and noradrenergic axons within the cerebral cortex, that these correlations extend for long distances (at least 3.5–4 millimeters), and that the major contributor to these correlations is a common signal related to behavioral state (e.g. uninstructed movements and arousal).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the correlation and coherence analyses.

claim: The residual, partial correlations that remain once the common signal is subtracted had a similar distribution to that of correlations between non-activity-dependent axons, indicating that these correlations may not represent behaviorally relevant signals.
source: The residual, partial correlations that remain once this common signal is subtracted had a similar distribution to that of correlations between non-activity-dependent axons, indicating that these correlations may not represent behaviorally relevant signals.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the partial correlation analysis results.

claim: While there is a broad range of correlations between modulatory axons, the study was unable to confirm that the range of correlations not explained by the global signal is representative of a heterogeneous signaling mechanism.
source: Thus, while there is a broad range of correlations between modulatory axons, we were unable to confirm that the range of correlations not explained by the global signal is representative of a heterogeneous signaling mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the limitations of the study in confirming heterogeneous signaling.

claim: Even though the average response of the ACh or NA axons may be similar for two different bouts of whisker movement, the pattern of activity generated within the simultaneously monitored ACh or NA axon segment can vary strongly.
source: Indeed, even though the average response of the ACh of NA axons may be similar for two different bouts of whisker movement, the pattern of activity generated within the simultaneously monitored ACh or NA axon segment can vary strongly.
evidence: This observation is based on analysis of trial-to-trial variability in axonal responses.

claim: A striking decrease in correlation between cholinergic (and noradrenergic) axon segments was observed during walking.
source: Indeed, we observed a striking decrease in correlation between cholinergic (and noradrenergic) axon segments during walking (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figure supplement.

claim: The same decrease in correlation during walking was obtained when comparing adjacent segments from the same axon, indicating that this movement-related decorrelation in fluorescence-based activity is most likely an artifact of frequency-limited fluorescence-based data collection methods.
source: However, we obtained the same result when comparing adjacent segments from the same axon (which should remain highly correlated throughout all behavioral states), indicating that this movement-related decorrelation in fluorescence-based activity is most likely an artifact of frequency-limited fluorescence-based data collection methods.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the control analysis of same-axon segments.

claim: The study is unable to measure whether there is, or is not, a decorrelation of biologically relevant activity between cholinergic and noradrenergic axons during walking or whisking because individual action potentials (or the resulting fluctuations in [Ca2+]i) within axons cannot be resolved at all frequencies.
source: Since we cannot resolve individual action potentials (or the resulting fluctuations in [Ca2+]i) within axons at all frequencies, we are unable to measure whether there is, or is not, a decorrelation of biologically relevant activity between these axons during walking or whisking.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the imaging method.

claim: Averaged activity across all recorded VCINs tracked changes in the animal's behavioral state.
source: Averaged activity across all recorded VCINs tracked changes in the animal's behavioral state.
evidence: This is a general observation from the VCIN data.

claim: Small whisker pad twitches were associated with a modest average increase in VCIN population activity, while longer whisking bouts and walking bouts were associated with larger increases in average population activity.
source: Small whisker pad twitches were associated with a modest average increase in VCIN population activity, while longer whisking bouts and walking bouts were associated with larger increases in average population activity (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: In similarity with both BF-ACh and LC-NA axons, VCIN activity quickly increased at the onset of facial movements and returned to baseline within 1–2 s following a return to stillness.
source: In similarity with both BF-ACh and LC-NA axons, VCIN activity quickly increased at the onset of facial movements and returned to baseline within 1–2 s following a return to stillness (Figure 5E).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Examining the relationship between whisking onset and VCIN GCaMP6s activity at an expanded time base revealed a slight (<150 ms) onset lag between whisking onset and VCIN GCaMP6s activity.
source: Examining the relationship between whisking onset and VCIN GCaMP6s activity at an expanded time base (Figure 5E, inset) revealed a slight (<150 ms) onset lag between whisking onset and VCIN GCaMP6s activity.
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: VCIN activation was less tightly coupled to the onset and offsets of walking bouts, likely due to facial movements consistently occurring prior to walking bout onsets and persisting after walking offset.
source: VCIN activation was less tightly coupled to the onset and offsets of walking bouts (Figure 5F), likely due to facial movements consistently occurring prior to walking bout onsets and persisting after walking offset (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed temporal relationships.

claim: The observed relationship between VCIN signaling and whisking and walking behaviors was prominent in only a subset of these neurons.
source: The observed relationship between VCIN signaling and whisking and walking behaviors was prominent in only a subset of these neurons (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: On any given whisking bout 43.0 ± 31.3% of VCINs responded significantly while on any given walking bout 27.2 ± 27.9% responded significantly.
source: On any given whisking bout 43.0 ± 31.3% of VCINs responded significantly while on any given walking bout 27.2 ± 27.9% responded significantly with this time period comparison.
evidence: This finding is based on analysis of the probability of VCIN responses to behavioral events.

claim: Correlation of activity between pairs of VCIN neurons varied from 0.43 to 0.96 and averaged 0.74 ± 0.12.
source: Correlation of activity between pairs of VCIN neurons varied from 0.43 to 0.96 and averaged 0.74 ± 0.12.
evidence: This finding is based on correlation analysis of VCIN activity.

claim: All (n = 18) of the adjacent cell body halves exhibited a correlation at, or near, 1 (minimum correlation = 0.91).
source: Indeed, all (n = 18) of the adjacent cell body halves exhibited a correlation at, or near, 1 (minimum correlation = 0.91; Figure 5K).
evidence: This finding is based on correlation analysis of same-cell body halves.

claim: There appeared to be no significant relationship between distance and correlation between VCIN GCaMP6s activity.
source: There appeared to be no significant relationship between distance and correlation between VCIN GCaMP6s activity (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is an observation from the correlation analysis.

claim: For neurons with ordinary correlations less than approximately 0.6, the residual partial correlation centered around approximately 0, suggesting that these neurons were correlated in their activity owing to co-correlation with a common signal.
source: For neurons with ordinary correlations less than approximately 0.6, the residual partial correlation centered around approximately 0, suggesting that these neurons were correlated in their activity owing to co-correlation with a common signal.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the partial correlation analysis results.

claim: A small number of neuronal pairs were strongly correlated in activity outside that associated with the common (average) VCIN activity.
source: This result suggests that this small number of neuronal pairs were strongly correlated in activity outside that associated with the common (average) VCIN activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the partial correlation analysis results.

claim: Calculating partial correlation between two halves of the same cell body, taking into account the average common activity of other simultaneously imaged neurons, did not reduce the correlation in VCINs (ordinary correlation: 0.99 ± 0.02, partial correlation: 0.99 ± 0.03; t = –1.35, p=0.20).
source: Calculating partial correlation between two halves of the same cell body, taking into account the average common activity of other simultaneously imaged neurons, did not reduce the correlation in VCINs (ordinary correlation: 0.99 ± 0.02, partial correlation: 0.99 ± 0.03; t = –1.35, p=0.20), an expected result since these two cell body halves should be highly correlated in all of their activity, including that remaining following removal of the group common signal correlation.
evidence: This finding is based on partial correlation analysis and statistical testing.

claim: Plotting the partial residual correlation between VCIN neurons as a function of distance revealed a small decrease with distance (r = –0.14; p<0.01), suggesting that nearby VCIN neurons are slightly more likely to be correlated outside the common signal than distant cells.
source: Plotting the partial residual correlation between VCIN neurons as a function of distance revealed a small decrease with distance (Figure 5M; r = –0.14; p<0.01), suggesting that nearby VCIN neurons are slightly more likely to be correlated outside the common signal than distant cells.
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figure and statistical analysis.

claim: In contrast to ACh axons, the reduction in correlation between VCIN neurons by taking into account a common signal was not dependent upon whisking or walking.
source: Interestingly, in contrast to ACh axons, the reduction in correlation between VCIN neurons by taking into account a common signal was not dependent upon whisking or walking (Figure 5N).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: BF-ACh and LC-NA activity across the cortex is strongly linked to changes in behavioral state, as indicated by externally observable measures (whisker/facial movements, pupil diameter, locomotion) with strong ACh/NA activations occurring during periods of behavioral engagement.
source: First, our results confirmed that BF-ACh and LC-NA activity across the cortex is strongly linked to changes in behavioral state, as indicated by externally observable measures (whisker/facial movements, pupil diameter, locomotion) with strong ACh/NA activations occurring during periods of behavioral engagement (Figures 1—4, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: Facial/whisker movement is a better predictor of BF-ACh and LC-NA activity than walking speed or pupil diameter.
source: Second, we found that facial/whisker movement is a better predictor of BF-ACh and LC-NA activity than walking speed or pupil diameter (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: ACh and NA axonal signaling is dominated by a global, arousal/movement-related signal.
source: Third, we found strong evidence that ACh and NA axonal signaling is dominated by a global, arousal/movement-related signal (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: There is evidence consistent with a weaker heterogeneous component of ACh and NA axonal signaling.
source: Fourth, we found evidence consistent with a weaker heterogeneous component of ACh and NA axonal signaling (Figure 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 1K–O).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: There is evidence for both behavior-linked and heterogeneous cortical ACh signaling via local cortical VIP-ChAT interneurons.
source: Finally, we presented evidence for both behavior-linked and heterogeneous cortical ACh signaling via local cortical VIP-ChAT interneurons (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: BF-ACh and LC-NA have long been implicated in initiating and maintaining the waking state and arousal.
source: BF-ACh and LC-NA have long been implicated in initiating and maintaining the waking state and arousal (Berridge, 2008; McCormick, 1989; Picciotto et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Activity of LC neurons is higher during waking compared to sleeping.
source: For example, activity of LC neurons is higher during waking compared to sleeping (Hobson et al., 1975), and increased LC activity occurs before the transition from sleep to awake (Aston-Jones and Bloom, 1981).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Increased LC activity occurs before the transition from sleep to awake.
source: For example, activity of LC neurons is higher during waking compared to sleeping (Hobson et al., 1975), and increased LC activity occurs before the transition from sleep to awake (Aston-Jones and Bloom, 1981).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of the LC induces a sleep–wake transition.
source: The potential causal role of the LC in regulation of wakefulness is supported by more recent experiments that have shown that optogenetic stimulation of the LC induces a sleep–wake transition (Carter et al., 2010; Hayat et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Noradrenergic signaling is associated with moment-to-moment fluctuations in arousal and behavioral engagement/vigilance within the waking state.
source: Noradrenergic signaling is also associated with moment-to-moment fluctuations in arousal and behavioral engagement/vigilance within the waking state (Joshi et al., 2016; Joshi and Gold, 2022); reviewed in (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Poe et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies and reviews.

claim: In the mouse, activity of noradrenergic axons in primary visual and auditory cortices tracks fluctuations in pupil diameter and orofacial movements.
source: In the mouse, activity of noradrenergic axons in primary visual and auditory cortices tracks fluctuations in pupil diameter and orofacial movements (Larsen and Waters, 2018; Reimer et al., 2016), which, in mice, are indicators of behavioral state (reviewed in McGinley et al., 2015b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Optogenetic activation of the LC induces pupil dilation while inhibition of the LC leads to pupil constriction.
source: Moreover, optogenetic activation of the LC induces pupil dilation while inhibition of the LC leads to pupil constriction (Breton-Provencher and Sur, 2019; Megemont et al., 2022; Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Early recordings from the LC in awake, behaving rodents or monkeys revealed tonic increases in average firing rate related to arousal and phasic, often synchronous, discharge associated with short-term increases in behavioral vigilance to external environment and stimuli.
source: Early recordings from the LC in awake, behaving rodents or monkeys revealed tonic increases in average firing rate related to arousal and phasic, often synchronous, discharge associated with short-term increases in behavioral vigilance to external environment and stimuli (reviewed in Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Sara, 2009; Sara and Bouret, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: More recent investigations reveal at least some degree of heterogeneity and specialization in LC neuronal signaling.
source: More recent investigations reveal at least some degree of heterogeneity and specialization in LC neuronal signaling (see below; Breton-Provencher et al., 2022; Chandler et al., 2014; Poe et al., 2020; Totah et al., 2019; Uematsu et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The observation of a common signal across noradrenergic axons related to behavioral state is consistent with a global noradrenergic influence on cortical and subcortical network activity related to behavioral arousal, engagement, and vigilance.
source: Our observation of a common signal across noradrenergic axons related to behavioral state (e.g. whisker movements – a general measure of behavioral engagement in mice) is consistent with a global noradrenergic influence on cortical and subcortical network activity related to behavioral arousal, engagement, and vigilance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings in the context of previous research.

claim: The basal forebrain cholinergic system has been associated with transition to the waking state from sleep.
source: Similar to the LC, the basal forebrain cholinergic system has been associated with transition to the waking state from sleep (Han et al., 2014; Irmak and de Lecea, 2014; Teles-Grilo Ruivo et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2015), as well as general cortical activation (Buzsaki et al., 1988; Metherate et al., 1992; Metherate and Ashe, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: During slow wave sleep, ACh release in the cortex and thalamus is substantially reduced compared to the waking state and REM sleep state.
source: During slow wave sleep, ACh release in the cortex and thalamus is substantially reduced compared to the waking state and REM sleep state (Lee et al., 2005; Williams et al., 1994) and stimulation of the cholinergic basal forebrain promotes wakefulness (Han et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2015; Zant et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Stimulation of the cholinergic basal forebrain promotes wakefulness.
source: During slow wave sleep, ACh release in the cortex and thalamus is substantially reduced compared to the waking state and REM sleep state (Lee et al., 2005; Williams et al., 1994) and stimulation of the cholinergic basal forebrain promotes wakefulness (Han et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2015; Zant et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the waking state, cortical cholinergic axonal activity fluctuates in relation to increases in behavioral arousal and engagement (as measured by the onset of whisker movements, increases in pupil diameter and locomotion).
source: In the waking state, cortical cholinergic axonal activity fluctuates in relation to increases in behavioral arousal and engagement (as measured by the onset of whisker movements, increases in pupil diameter and locomotion) (Eggermann et al., 2014; Nelson and Mooney, 2016; Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Activation of the basal forebrain cholinergic system appears to be particularly important for the suppression of spontaneous slow oscillations in cortical and thalamocortical activity, which are characteristic of behavioral quiescence or drowsiness.
source: Activation of the basal forebrain cholinergic system appears to be particularly important for the suppression of spontaneous slow oscillations in cortical and thalamocortical activity, which are characteristic of behavioral quiescence or drowsiness (Eggermann et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The observation of a global common signal in cholinergic axons correlated with measures of behavioral engagement, particularly movements of the whiskers and face, supports the view that one of the major roles of the basal forebrain cholinergic system is to provide a broad modulation of the neocortex in association with moment-to-moment changes in behavioral state, including arousal, engagement, vigilance, and attention.
source: Our observation of a global common signal in cholinergic axons correlated with measures of behavioral engagement, particularly movements of the whiskers and face, supports the view that one of the major roles of the basal forebrain cholinergic system is to provide a broad modulation of the neocortex in association with moment-to-moment changes in behavioral state, including arousal, engagement, vigilance, and attention.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings in the context of previous research.

claim: A recent study of dopaminergic axons within the mouse cortex revealed state-dependent activity very similar to that observed for cholinergic and noradrenergic axons, including increases in activity with whisker movement, pupil dilation, and locomotion.
source: Interestingly, a recent study of dopaminergic axons within the mouse cortex also revealed state-dependent activity very similar to that observed here for cholinergic and noradrenergic axons, including increases in activity with whisker movement, pupil dilation, and locomotion (Figure 4 in Sturgill et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Studies of multiple cell types throughout the cortex, thalamus, and other structures reveal frequent coordinated rapid shifts in neural dynamics throughout the mouse brain during the waking state that are highly coordinated with rapid changes in behavioral state.
source: These results, along with studies of multiple cell types throughout the cortex, thalamus, and other structures (McCormick et al., 2020; McGinley et al., 2015b; Musall et al., 2019; Nestvogel and McCormick, 2022; Steinmetz et al., 2019; Stringer et al., 2019), reveal frequent coordinated rapid shifts in neural dynamics throughout the mouse brain during the waking state that are highly coordinated with rapid changes in behavioral state.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The coordinated shift in neural dynamics across broad regions of the brain, including neuromodulatory pathways, does not preclude important regional and temporal variations in activity that are specific to each pathway/system.
source: This coordinated shift in neural dynamics across broad regions of the brain, including neuromodulatory pathways, does not preclude important regional and temporal variations in activity that are specific to each pathway/system.
evidence: This is a general statement about the interpretation of the findings.

claim: The activation of the basal forebrain cholinergic pathways remains sustained throughout prolonged bouts of movement, whereas the noradrenergic system from the locus coeruleus is more transient – mainly signaling the onset of a period of behavioral engagement.
source: For example, we have shown here that the activation of the basal forebrain cholinergic pathways remains sustained throughout prolonged bouts of movement, whereas the noradrenergic system from the locus coeruleus is more transient – mainly signaling the onset of a period of behavioral engagement (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding from the study.

claim: The cholinergic system is more associated with alteration in brain dynamics associated with sustained engagement with the external world, while the noradrenergic input may be more related to the behavioral transition to external engagement.
source: This result suggests that the cholinergic system is more associated with alteration in brain dynamics associated with sustained engagement with the external world, while the noradrenergic input may be more related to the behavioral transition to external engagement (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Clayton et al., 2004; Poe et al., 2020; Reimer et al., 2016; Vazey et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Revealing the unique spatiotemporal features of each neuromodulatory system will be critical to understanding how each contributes to the control of neural dynamics in the waking state.
source: Revealing the unique spatiotemporal features of each neuromodulatory system will be critical to understanding how each contributes to the control of neural dynamics in the waking state.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of future research.

claim: ACh and LC-NA may also provide heterogeneous signals throughout the brain that support a range of brain processes and behaviors, including selective sensory processing, cortical plasticity, and memory formation.
source: In addition to a global behavioral state-linked signal, ACh and LC-NA may also provide heterogeneous signals throughout the brain. These targeted signals may support a range of brain processes and behaviors, including selective sensory processing, cortical plasticity, and memory formation (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Breton-Provencher et al., 2022; Deitcher et al., 2019; Ego-Stengel et al., 2001; Goard and Dan, 2009; Janitzky et al., 2015; Nelson and Mooney, 2016; Pinto et al., 2013; Polack et al., 2013; Sara, 2009; Sara and Bouret, 2012; Uematsu et al., 2017; Usher et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Specificity of cholinergic cortical signaling has been demonstrated both anatomically and functionally.
source: Specificity of cholinergic cortical signaling has been demonstrated both anatomically and functionally.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the subsequent specific examples provided in the text.

claim: Inputs and outputs of cholinergic neurons in the BF are topographically organized.
source: Inputs and outputs of cholinergic neurons in the BF are topographically organized (Gielow and Zaborszky, 2017; Zaborszky et al., 2015) and activating distinct regions of the BF results in desynchronization of restricted cortical regions (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Recent work has demonstrated heterogeneity in cortical ACh receptor activation, particularly during periods of locomotion.
